common_name: Kiowa Pecan (Precocious Large-Nut Type I Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Kiowa is a Type I (protandrous) pollen shedder, so plant alongside a Type II variety such as Choctaw, Caddo, or Cheyenne for reliable cross-pollination and nut set. Kiowa begins bearing unusually young for a pecan, often within 4-6 years of planting.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with room for a large mature canopy. Kiowa is an Oklahoma State University release prized by home orchardists for its precocity, bearing well ahead of most named pecan varieties, and for its very large, attractive, thin-shelled nuts with excellent bright kernel color and good fill. It is a Type I pollinator, so pair it with a Type II variety for cross-pollination and heavier yields. Scab pressure is moderate; in the humid Gulf South a fungicide program during wet springs helps protect nut quality, while drier inland sites see less trouble. Thin overcrowded nut clusters in heavy-bearing years to reduce alternate bearing and keep nut size consistent season to season.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Pecan Variety Recommendations
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
LSU AgCenter — Pecan Production in Louisiana

common_name: Sioux Pecan (High Kernel-Percentage Type I Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Sioux is a Type I pollen shedder, so pair it with a Type II variety such as Choctaw, Caddo, or Elliott for cross-pollination. Its more compact growth habit than most pecans suits smaller home orchard spacing at the tighter end of the range.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sioux, released from the USDA breeding program in Texas, produces small to medium nuts but is valued for an exceptionally high kernel percentage and rich, sweet flavor that makes it a favorite among home growers for eating fresh out of hand. Its smaller, more manageable tree size compared to old-line pecans like Stuart makes it a good fit for home orchards with limited space. It is a Type I pollinator and needs a Type II variety nearby for good nut set. Scab susceptibility is a real concern in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so Sioux performs best in drier inland areas or with a fungicide spray program during wet springs; irrigate deeply during nut fill for the best kernel quality.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Pecan Breeding Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection
Oklahoma State University Extension — Pecan Variety Recommendations

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southland is self-fertile and ripens mid-season in the Gulf South, a reliable middle-of-the-pack variety to fill out the harvest window between early and late black muscadines.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Southland is a University of Georgia release valued for its large, dark reddish-black berries with a thin skin and sweet, rich muscadine flavor good for fresh eating as well as juice and wine. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and consistently productive, with solid disease resistance across the humid Gulf South. Mid-season ripening makes Southland a dependable companion to earlier black varieties like Cowart and later ones like Ison, spreading harvest over a longer window. Prune annually in late winter while dormant to renewal spurs to keep the vine productive and manageable on the trellis.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Georgia
Mississippi State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Production
LSU AgCenter Publication — Muscadines for Louisiana Home Gardens

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Black Beauty is self-fertile and ripens over an extended late-summer window, so pick over successive weeks rather than in a single harvest.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Black Beauty is a University of Arkansas release bred specifically for fresh-market eating, producing very large, glossy black berries with a tender skin and mild, sweet flavor that is less musky than many older muscadine varieties. It is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though nearby vines improve fruit set. Vigor is strong and disease resistance is good across the humid Gulf South. Because berries ripen unevenly over several weeks rather than all at once, plan on repeated picking passes through the harvest season for the best quality fruit.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Muscadine Grape Breeding Program
LSU AgCenter Publication — Muscadines for Louisiana Home Gardens
Mississippi State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Production

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Late Fry is self-fertile and, true to its name, ripens near the very end of the muscadine season, extending harvest well past earlier black varieties like Cowart.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Late Fry is a University of Arkansas release bred as a black-fruited counterpart to the popular bronze variety Fry, producing very large, glossy black berries with the same thin skin and high sugar content that made Fry a favorite for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and ripens late in the season, filling out the tail end of the muscadine harvest after earlier black varieties are finished. Vigor and disease resistance are good across the humid Gulf South. Because it is one of the last muscadines to ripen, protect ripening clusters from birds and other wildlife, which concentrate on the few varieties still fruiting late in the season.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Muscadine Grape Breeding Program
LSU AgCenter Publication — Muscadines for Louisiana Home Gardens
Mississippi State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Production
